analysis.one_liner: Repeals major Affordable Care Act coverage rules and lets insurers sell plans across state lines under home-state rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat with three House committees and its subcommittees and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal Title I of the Affordable Care Act — the rules that guarantee people with pre-existing conditions can buy coverage, require plans to cover a standard set of benefits, and provide tax credits through the marketplaces. It would then let each health insurer pick a single "primary" state as its regulator and sell individual policies in every other state under that state's rules, exempting them from the consumer protections of the states where their customers live. Buyers would see a bold-print notice that their policy may skip benefits and consumer protections required by their own state.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, which could choose the state with the fewest coverage requirements and sell minimally regulated plans nationwide, and healthy buyers, who would likely see lower premiums because plans would no longer have to cover essential benefits or charge sick and healthy people similar rates.

how_it_helps.text: By repealing Title I of the Affordable Care Act, the bill would remove the requirements for guaranteed issue, essential health benefits, and the marketplace tax credits that subsidize individual coverage [S2].

It would let an insurer designate one primary state whose laws govern its individual policies everywhere, and would exempt the issuer from secondary states' laws regulating its operation, so a plan could be sold in any state while following only its home state's rules [S3].

Supporters argued in the bill's findings that state mandates and federal rules raise the cost of individual coverage, and that letting insurers sell across state lines would make cheaper plans available [S3].

The bill did keep some protections: insurers could not reclassify a person or raise their premium at renewal based on health status, out-of-state plans would need an independent medical review process for denied claims, and the primary state had to use a risk-based capital formula [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions and older buyers, who would lose guaranteed access to standard-benefit coverage and could be priced out or pushed into stripped-down plans, and marketplace enrollees, who would lose the tax credits that lower their premiums.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Title I would end the guarantee that people with pre-existing conditions can buy coverage, the requirement that plans cover a standard set of benefits, and the tax credits that subsidize marketplace coverage [S2].

Out-of-state plans would be exempt from the secondary state's consumer protections and restrictions on rate changes; the buyer's only safeguard would be a bold-print notice warning that the policy may cover less and is not subject to the state's protections [S3].

Because each issuer picks its own primary state, the structure rewards selling from the state with the fewest coverage requirements, which could pull the cheapest, thinnest plans into every state [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Healthy buyers would likely pay less, and the bill preserved renewal protections against health-status repricing and an external appeals process. But the cost falls on the people who most need insurance: repealing Title I removes guaranteed issue, essential benefits, and premium subsidies, and the out-of-state plans are deliberately allowed to skip a state's coverage mandates and rate rules, with only a disclosure notice to warn the buyer. The savings for the healthy come largely from shifting risk onto the sick and the old.

outcome.mechanism: After being introduced it was referred to three House committees and then to their health subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on January 27, 2015, with 18 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support [S1].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees, and in early 2015 to their health subcommittees; the record shows no markup, no vote, and no further action after April 2015 [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 114th Congress in January 2017 without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with pre-existing conditions, older buyers, and marketplace enrollees kept the Affordable Care Act's coverage guarantees and subsidies, and state insurance regulators kept their authority over plans sold to their residents; insurers never got the ability to sell minimally regulated plans nationwide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sick and older buyers kept ACA protections

for.name: Rep. Marsha Blackburn
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 18 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 18 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored [S4]; the bill died in committee without a recorded vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: Under the bill, insurers could designate the state with the weakest coverage requirements as their regulator and sell plans in every other state exempt from that state's consumer protections and rate rules, competing by selling thinner coverage. The gain comes from selling less protective plans, which shifts costs onto sick and older customers.

The bill gives the issuer's chosen primary state sole jurisdiction to enforce its rules and exempts insurers from most secondary states' insurance laws, stripping states of their traditional power to regulate plans sold to their own residents. The GAO would study the effects for five years, but the secondary states' role would be reduced to taxes, financial exams, fraud, and claims-practice enforcement [S3].
